title.narrative: ERSKID/KIB/DAU/01/Enhanced implementation of the Degree of Urbanisation (DEGURBA) city definition approach in selected countries

description.narrative:
Historically, many countries use different criteria to define urban and rural areas which reflect their various perspectives as to what constitutes such areas. Individual countries need to have their own national definitions that can be implemented in their statistical systems and used to disaggregate indicators by urban and rural areas for their own national policy purposes. Nevertheless, to have meaningful international comparisons of statistical indicators along this continuum, there is also an undisputed need for a definition that is nationally relevant and internationally comparable at the same time.
Since 2015, the global urban community welcomed two global agendas, namely the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the New Urban Agenda (NUA). Within the SDGs, the international community recognized urbanization and city growth as a transformative force for development by endorsing a goal on cities (Goal 11)–make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient, and sustainable. This goal was further reinforced by the adoption of the 2016 New Urban Agenda in Quito—which is an urbanization action blueprint for member states, UN-Habitat and other UN agencies, civil society, communities, the private sector, professionals, the scientific and academic community. The SDGs also introduced a new reporting territorial level—the city, for which more than half of the SDG targets have an urban component. This not only places cities and urban areas at the center of the SDGs framework, but also demands collection of data at the urban level and/or disaggregation of reporting between urban and rural levels. Producing comparable data at the urban level requires clear definitions on what constitutes a city, as well as globally applicable metrics/ thresholds that can be applied across countries and cities that report either via the Voluntary National Review (VNR) reports or the Voluntary Local Review (VLR) reports. Since the adoption of the MDGs and then the SDGs, attainment of a globally agreed city definition has proven elusive, and a key challenge to the generation of urban specific data, and in turn affecting the comparable reporting on related indicators. During the United Nations Conference on Housing and Sustainable Urban Development (Habitat III) held in Quito, Ecuador in 2016, a voluntary commitment was made by the European Commission, the World Bank, FAO, and OECD to develop a harmonized and people-based approach to defining cities and human settlements. In 2018, UN-Habitat joined the voluntary commitment with the objective of ensuring deliberations responded to urban monitoring needs of the agency and member states including other urban partners and actors. Between 2018 and 2019, UN-Habitat and the European Commission successfully implemented a project titled “Assessing the feasibility of applying a global definition of cities/urban areas in support of global monitoring of SDGs and NUA urban targets”, through which the Degree of Urbanization concept (DEGURBA) to urban/rural areas definition was introduced to 250 participants from 85 countries through regional consultative workshops held in Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC), Arab States and Asia and the Pacific regions . Following these consultative workshops, UN member states, during the 51st UN Statistical Commission meeting (March 2020) endorsed DEGURBA as a sound approach to defining urban and rural areas for statistical comparisons. With this endorsement came the major need to provide support to countries on its local application, as well to build their capacities on the application of DEGURBA including how to generate boundaries for SDG 11 monitoring and reporting. From all the workshops conducted, these two needs were identified as action areas needed to further the roll-out of DEGURBA after the endorsement. The current project, which is almost an extension from the previous project, aims to respond to the identified needs for enhancing capacity for countries to implement DEGURBA at the local level and use it to produce harmonized data against the SDG 11 targets. While targeting only 13 countries, implementation of the project in these countries will have a major ripple effect, with lessons learnt disseminated globally. Country to country learning on the benefits of DEGURBA and on-the-job training on SDG 11 data production is also anticipated to enhance urban monitoring at the local level.
